queue.title: Spec loop R1 -- explore and propose
queue.detail: DONE, iteration 4. openspec/changes/2026-09-10-the-control-that-asks-holds-the-keyboard/ -- proposal.md, design.md, tasks.md, and deltas against TWO capabilities: hub-interaction-feedback (2 ADDED requirements -- Escape arbitration, and focus after a menu selection) and task-lifecycle-governance (1 MODIFIED requirement). openspec validate --strict passes; openspec list reads 3 deltas / 30 tasks. The argument: F309 and F310 are one failure -- two mechanisms act on one keystroke and the one further from the operator wins. The fix is arbitration in both halves: useDialogFocus stands down on an Escape that is already defaultPrevented, and a RowMenu item that opens a control expecting input tells the menu not to take focus back. R1 found a THIRD instance of F310 nobody has driven (DirectoryPicker.tsx:57-62 inside ProjectManagerModal.tsx:157-166, whose useDialogFocus is active at :73), and it turned an ADDED delta into a MODIFIED one by grepping first: task-lifecycle-governance already ships 'A control offering the waiting status collects the statement' and the product obeys it. F307 is explicitly NOT subsumed, with the three reasons and the one reverse dependency written into the proposal. One link was deliberately not measured (whether autoFocus fires and is overridden, or never fires) and the fix is specified so the answer does not matter.

queue.title: Spec loop R2 -- re-derive against the code
queue.detail: DONE, iteration 5, and it did not come back empty. THE FINDING: R1's task-lifecycle-governance delta added a scenario reading 'the operator moves a task to the waiting status without using a pointer at any point', which is more than the change delivers -- reaching the drawer's status menu from the keyboard means Tab-walking the board's remaining controls behind the scrim, which is F307, and design.md D8 excludes F307 deliberately. Archiving that delta would have written a false current-behaviour statement into openspec/specs/. The requirement is KEPT (D6 settled: it is the only rule that names what the operator loses on a path the Hub makes mandatory) but NARROWED to 'the keyboard is in the control asking what the task is waiting for, once the menu has closed', and tasks.md 7.6 drives exactly that while forbidding an implementer from re-widening it. ALSO: the focus-steal mechanism was read out of the dependency instead of described loosely -- there are TWO actors (DropdownMenuContent's own composed onCloseAutoFocus at react-dropdown-menu:113-117, and FocusScope's restore at react-focus-scope:89-98), one preventDefault suppresses both because composeEventHandlers defaults to checkForDefaultPrevented: true, and the steal runs inside a setTimeout(0), which is the precise reason D5's 'no setTimeout' is right. ALSO: tasks.md 7.2/7.3's exact-count acceptance contract was self-contradictory (7.4 and 7.5 add legs to the same two harnesses) and the harness's D2 leg skips silently without failing -- both counts are now floors, with 7.2a naming the skip hazard. Confirmed unchanged: the capture-flag ordering at exact lines, the seven-Escape-owner boundary re-derived by grep, the six call sites and six mount sites, and the MODIFIED requirement's byte-fidelity. Three of R1's line citations were off by a few lines and were corrected.

queue.title: Spec loop R3 -- re-derive again, independently
queue.detail: DONE, iteration 6, and it did not come back empty either -- three rounds, three rounds that changed the proposal. THE FINDING: R1 and R2 both concluded that the third instance of F310 (DirectoryPicker inside ProjectManagerModal) was repaired by task 1.1 without an edit, because the picker already calls preventDefault() at :57-62. It cannot be. That handler is a React onKeyDown bound to the picker's root div (:85-91, tabIndex=-1) and nothing in the file ever focuses that root; opening the browser leaves focus on the Browse... button, a SIBLING of the picker (ProjectManagerModal.tsx:153 vs :157-166), so React never dispatches through the picker's subtree, preventDefault() never runs, and 1.1's defaultPrevented condition is false. The modal closes and takes the browser with it -- same visible cost as F310, different mechanism, which is why two rounds reading for outcome agreed on the wrong one. The change's own D3 had already argued exactly this in the opposite direction ('focus is frequently not inside the panel at all'). Written up as design.md D9: arbitration by defaultPrevented presumes the nested owner HOLDS THE KEYBOARD, and the precondition differs by mechanism -- Radix binds document/capture and is focus-independent, while a React onKeyDown only fires for a target inside its own subtree. Consequence for the other instance: the reason input's handler works only because task 4.1 focuses it, so the F310 half DEPENDS ON the F309 half -- now task 2.1a, because an implementer landing 1.1 and 2.1 alone would watch leg C3 still fail with no reason to suspect the focus work. Fix chosen over narrowing the scenario: 2.2 focuses the picker root on open (it already carries role=dialog and tabIndex=-1), 2.2a returns focus to the trigger on close so the repair does not import F307's shape, and 2.2b plus a D8 carve-out stop it being read as the general F307 fix. SECOND FINDING: the delta scenario 'Typing an answer does not operate the menu' had NO task producing its evidence in any round, and its second clause ('no part of the surface becomes unresponsive to the pointer') is FALSE of the correctly fixed product -- TaskDetailDrawer renders a fixed inset-0 scrim at :195-209 that deliberately makes the board unresponsive and that its own click-outside listener depends on. Narrowed to 'does not stop answering the pointer BECAUSE A MENU RE-OPENED over it', and given evidence by a new task 7.8 (the rowmenu harness's PROBE already reads both facts); 7.8a records that leg P5 is NOT that evidence, because it focuses the trigger by hand and passes before and after. ALSO: 7.4 rewritten to name the focus state it must drive FROM -- without clicking inside the browser first, since a leg that clicks a breadcrumb would pass against an unfixed picker; 7.4a added as the mutation-check for the task two rounds denied was needed; 7.4b drives 2.2a. ALSO (b): six existing hub-interaction-feedback requirements, not five, all read as bodies -- R2's 'all about appearance' verdict survives and neither ADDED requirement collides, but 'Keyboard focus is visible' is a shipped requirement that 4.1's swap from autoFocus to a programmatic .focus() is one implementation away from breaching, so 4.1a guards it and 7.6 drives it. openspec validate --strict passes; openspec list reads 0/40 tasks, up from 32.

queue.title: Repairs that need no spec -- DONE at iteration 8: F313, the ledger's confession read as a verdict
queue.detail: DONE, iteration 8, and measuring first changed the target. The named candidate ('status lines that are blank or whose first word is prose') measured SMALLER than stated: 273 Status declarations, 149 leading 'open', 108 some spelling of 'fixed', 12 prose, and ZERO blank -- day-1's '22 blank' had counted headings with no status line, almost all of which the classifier merges into their parent at no cost. So I read the EVIDENCE behind every CONFLICT instead of the count of them. F313: seven of the eight conflicts were false and four were SELF-INFLICTED -- the corrections table blind spot 5 wrote on 2026-09-08 to record its own wrong verdicts was read as MAKING them, because the cross-section arm credits a verdict word to every finding number on the line. Fix dee508c: a line naming more than one finding number is bookkeeping about the ledger, not a verdict in it. 11 verdicts move over 312 sections, NONE toward resolved; for five of the eleven the new verdict is the one that table's own 'Now' column already records. Mutation-checked both directions (disable -> new guard fails; widen to >=1 -> narrowness pin AND the pre-existing CONFLICT test fail). SECOND, separate defect, 2dd6807: F291's status line reads '**still open**' and the census counted it RESOLVED, because in_res outranks in_open and the weak arm fired on 'not a defect with an obvious fix' -- a clause about the FIX. Reworded, F291 is OPEN. F12/F53/F149 given leading tokens the classifier reads off the declaration. The eight 'not a defect' lines left alone on purpose: promoting them to a STRONG token would inflate the arm the script's own header calls not fully trustworthy. THE LESSON, and it is in the entry: writing F313 REPRODUCED F313 -- one draft sentence naming F65 beside 'resolved' put F65 back to CONFLICT, so the rule is a floor and not a cure. The defence is to re-run the classifier after appending and require that no existing verdict moves.

The trap R2 found is worth generalising, and D-5 should describe its shape: a proposal can be right about the code and still write a DELTA THAT CLAIMS MORE THAN THE CHANGE DELIVERS. The over-claim rides in on a scenario's WHEN clause rather than on any statement about the code, so a round that only re-checks source citations cannot see it. The test that catches it is: name the task that produces this scenario's evidence, then ask whether it can.

R3 (iteration 6) generalised the trap R2 found, and D-5 should state the general form once: a proposal can be right about the code and still write a delta that CLAIMS MORE THAN THE CHANGE DELIVERS (R2's finding, and R3's DirectoryPicker finding) or that a SHIPPED BEHAVIOUR CONTRADICTS (R3's scrim finding). Neither rides in on a statement about the code, so a round that only re-checks source citations cannot see either. The test that catches both: name the task that produces this scenario's evidence and ask whether it CAN -- then, if the answer is yes, ask what already-shipped behaviour would make the scenario false.

A round that re-reads what the previous round already re-read is the low-yield round. R2 re-derived R1's source citations and they held; R3 was told not to repeat that and to attack the deltas instead, and found the change's largest defect inside a file R2 had also opened.
